newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - National Rail wants transport equality.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - National Rail wants transport equality.

text.p: Private sector involvement in Australia's rail industry would force a debate about creating a level playing field for road and rail operators, the head of the government-owned National Rail Corp, Vince Graham, said.

The key issues facing the two industries were unequal road and rail access fees, the different criteria for investment and the different tax and regulatory regimes they face, Graham told Reuters in an interview.

"For a long time the rail industry has complained about the amount of money being invested in roads and the road industry has complained about the taxpayer losses of the railways," he said. "All in all it has been a simple debate about who had their nose more deeply in to the taxpayers' trough."
Graham said the two modes of transport were becoming much more complementary in terms of understanding their strengths and competitive advantages against each other.
Behind this was the national competition policy and the provision of open access to private operators, Graham said.
"The establishment of National Rail itself has been a catalyst for reform of the industry," he said.
Graham said National Rail had demonstrated that rail was not the burden on the taxpayer that it historically had been, that it could be a successful commercial business.
The greater involvement of the private sector was positive as investor interest in rail was now a lot broader, Graham said.
"The fact that the private sector is in there means they are going to seek to influence rail policy as they've done for road policy for a long time. That's got to be a good thing for rail."
Graham said the policy debate that was likely to emerge would be about achieving competitive neutrality or a level playing field across four areas of transport.

The most significant issue was access payments. The road industry pays to use the road system through registration charges while rail industry pays access prices to run trains over the railway network.

"There is an enormous inequity in the regimes and the price of hauling a ton of freight on road to a tonne of freight on rail," he said. Graham said NRC paid A$115 million nationwide to run its transport over the national rail highway.
"The same transport task run on the national road highway would lead to registration charges of A$17 million," he said.
Graham said the road industry argued that it paid its way by virtue of the fuel excise tax.
"Rail also pays the same fuel excise charges and sees none it return in any way shape or form returning to its infrastructure," he said.
The second area of debate was the amount of infrastructure investment in the different areas and whether these investments were subject to the same economic criteria.
A third area of competitive neutrality was taxation.

"We are building new locomotives at the moment and paying no sales tax on them. If the road industry goes out there to buy a new B-double truck they pay 22.5 percent sales tax. That is an area where rail is advantaged and road is disadvantaged."
The final area of interest was regulation, Graham said.
While there was a strong push in the road industry for self regulation, the rail industry applied stringent safety standards that were not present in the road industry, Graham said.
"Presumably they (the road transport industry) are going to have a competitive interest in ensuring that these things are competitively neutral between modes," Graham said.
